description: Local evidence corpus for the workshop. All documents are synthetic teaching material. Documents with origin 'Course transcript summary' paraphrase the course transcripts; the rest are fictional briefing notes. DOC-17 is an adversarial test document.

documents.title: Chat assistants for routine student enquiries
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: In a fictional pilot at Northfield University, a chat assistant answered routine questions about deadlines, fees and timetables. The assistant only answered from an approved knowledge base maintained by student-services staff. Questions about appeals, wellbeing or financial hardship were escalated to a human adviser. Staff in the pilot reported fewer repetitive emails, which freed time for complex cases. The main risk observed was outdated knowledge-base content, which produced wrong deadline answers until content owners updated it.

documents.title: Early-alert analytics for student support
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Early-alert systems combine signals such as attendance, learning-platform activity and assignment submissions to flag students who may need support. In the fictional Northfield design, a flag only prompts an adviser to reach out; the adviser decides what to do. False positives are common, so flags should be treated as prompts for a conversation rather than conclusions. Students should be told what data is used, and the system must not be used for punitive decisions. Privacy, consent and transparency were identified as preconditions for trust.

documents.title: Agentic workflows for administrative processes
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Administrative processes such as transcript requests and scholarship applications involve several steps. An agentic workflow can gather the submitted documents, check completeness against a checklist, and draft a reply. A human officer approves any decision before it is sent to the student. In the fictional pilot, turnaround time for complete applications fell because missing documents were detected earlier. Every step was written to an audit log so that decisions could be reviewed later.

documents.title: Accessibility and inclusion in AI student services
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: AI assistants can offer multilingual support and 24-hour availability, which helps part-time and international students. Interfaces should work with screen readers and should not depend on high-bandwidth connections. A digital divide remains, so a human service channel must stay available. Answer quality should be evaluated separately for different student groups to detect uneven performance.

documents.title: Clinical documentation assistance
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Documentation assistants draft clinical notes from consultation recordings or clinician dictation. The clinician reviews, corrects and signs the note, so responsibility stays with the clinician. Potential benefits include less time spent on paperwork and more time with patients. A key risk is that drafts can contain details that were never said, so every draft must be verified before it enters the record.

documents.title: Decision support and triage
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: AI decision-support tools can estimate risk scores or highlight regions of interest in medical images. In many jurisdictions such tools are regulated as medical devices and need formal validation. Performance measured on one population may not transfer to another, a problem known as dataset shift. Local validation and ongoing monitoring are therefore needed before and after deployment.

documents.title: Patient-facing assistants
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Patient-facing assistants can schedule appointments, send medication reminders and answer general administrative questions. They should not provide diagnoses and must escalate urgent or clinical questions to qualified staff. Clear guardrails and escalation rules are required because incorrect advice can cause harm. Patients should always know when they are interacting with an automated system.

documents.title: Data governance and equity in health AI
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Health data is highly sensitive, so patient privacy, consent and data-protection law shape what systems can be built. Models trained on unrepresentative data can perform worse for under-represented groups. Organisations need clear accountability for AI-assisted decisions and processes to monitor systems after deployment. Equity audits should compare performance across patient groups.

documents.title: Customer service automation for small firms
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Small firms receive many repetitive questions such as 'where is my order?'. An agent with read-only access to the order database can look up order status and draft an answer. In a fictional case, a family bakery used such an agent for order-status and opening-hours questions, and passed refund requests to the owner. Human handoff for complaints and refunds protected customer relationships.

documents.title: Back-office agents for invoices and bookkeeping
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Agents can extract fields such as vendor, invoice number and due date from incoming invoices and match them to purchase orders. They can flag invoices that are close to their due date so that payments are not missed. The owner should approve payments; the agent should not move money on its own. Ambiguous date formats such as 04/05/2025 are a common source of extraction errors.

documents.title: Marketing content and inventory suggestions
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Language models can draft product descriptions and short social-media captions for a small shop. An agent that reads sales and stock data can suggest reorder quantities for fast-selling items. The owner reviews suggestions before ordering and edits content to keep a consistent brand voice. Short, specific captions tend to be easier to review and reuse.

documents.title: Adoption barriers for small businesses
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Barriers to adoption include cost, limited technical skills, poor data quality and low trust in automated decisions. Dependence on a single vendor (lock-in) is a further concern. A practical strategy is to start with one well-defined workflow, measure its performance before and after, and expand only if the results justify it.

documents.title: Crop monitoring with imagery
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Drone and satellite imagery can reveal crop stress, nutrient deficiency and early signs of disease. Image models need calibration for local crops, soils and growing seasons. Limited rural connectivity can delay data upload and analysis. Farmers benefit most when alerts come with a recommended action rather than a raw map.

documents.title: Advisory assistants for farmers
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Advisory assistants can answer farmers' questions about planting dates, pest management and fertiliser use through SMS or voice in local languages. Answers should be grounded in content verified by agronomists. Incorrect advice can be costly because it affects a whole season's harvest. Escalation to an extension officer should be available for unusual problems.

documents.title: Precision irrigation and resource use
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: Soil-moisture sensors combined with weather forecasts can schedule irrigation more precisely. In a fictional cooperative pilot, members reported using less water for the same yield, although results varied by field. Sensors need regular maintenance and calibration, which adds cost. Resource savings are a strong motivation where water is scarce.

documents.title: Supply chain and market information
documents.origin: Synthetic briefing note written for this workshop (fictional; not a published source)
documents.text: AI tools can give smallholder farmers price information for nearby markets and help plan transport. Better logistics planning can reduce post-harvest losses. Access barriers include the cost of smartphones, data charges and digital literacy. Cooperatives can share tools so that individual farmers do not carry the full cost.

documents.title: Direct generation versus agentic workflows
documents.origin: Course transcript summary (paraphrases the instructor-supplied transcript) - Module 1, Part 2
documents.text: A traditional (non-agentic) workflow asks a language model to produce the whole output in one pass, like writing an essay from start to finish without backspacing. An agentic workflow breaks the task into steps: for example, write an outline, decide what to research, gather sources, write a first draft, then review and revise it. The iterative process takes longer but often produces better results. The lecturer defines an agentic AI workflow as a process where an LLM-based app executes multiple steps to complete a task.

documents.title: Degrees of autonomy
documents.origin: Course transcript summary (paraphrases the instructor-supplied transcript) - Module 1, Part 3
documents.text: The lecture treats 'agentic' as an adjective describing a spectrum rather than a yes-or-no label. Less autonomous agents follow a sequence of steps hardcoded by the programmer, while the model fills in text at each step. Highly autonomous agents decide for themselves which steps to take and which tools to use. Less autonomous systems are more predictable and easier to control; more autonomous systems are more flexible but harder to control.

documents.title: Benefits reported in the lecture
documents.origin: Course transcript summary (paraphrases the instructor-supplied transcript) - Module 1, Part 4
documents.text: The lecture reports a coding benchmark (HumanEval) on which GPT-3.5 answered directly scored 40% and GPT-4 answered directly scored 67%. According to the lecture, wrapping GPT-3.5 in an agentic workflow produced an improvement larger than the jump from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4. Other benefits mentioned are parallelism, such as fetching several web pages at once, and modularity, such as swapping in a better search tool or model for one step.

documents.title: Evaluation and error analysis
documents.origin: Course transcript summary (paraphrases the instructor-supplied transcript) - Module 1 Part 7 and Module 4
documents.text: The lecture argues that the ability to drive a disciplined evaluation and error-analysis process is one of the strongest predictors of success when building agents. Developers should build a quick prototype, inspect outputs, and create small evaluation sets. Examining traces step by step shows which component causes failures; in one lecture example, search terms were unsatisfactory 5% of the time but search results 45% of the time.

documents.title: Agentic design patterns
documents.origin: Course transcript summary (paraphrases the instructor-supplied transcript) - Module 1, Part 8
documents.text: The course presents four design patterns: reflection, tool use, planning and multi-agent collaboration. Reflection asks a model to critique and improve its own output; tool use lets a model request functions such as web search or code execution. Planning lets the model decide the sequence of steps; multi-agent systems split work across specialised roles. Planning and multi-agent systems are more powerful but less predictable.
